newsitem.title: FRANCE: Suez, Lyonnaise finalise results amid merger talks.
newsitem.headline: Suez, Lyonnaise finalise results amid merger talks.

text.p: Suez and Lyonnaise des Eaux will polish what could be their last separate annual accounts this week as negotiations advance towards a merger that would create one of France's top conglomerates.
French newspapers reported at the weekend that the two sprawling companies had agreed on the basic shape of a merger to go before special board meetings now scheduled for April 11.
But key details, including the size of any sweetener for Suez shareholders, to be shared from its five billion franc cash pile, still stood in the way of a final deal, reports said.
Ominously for the two firms, which failed to agree on a merger two years ago, one newspaper said the whole match could be called off if Suez investors demanded too high a price.
"A common meeting ground must be found," Le Monde said in its Sunday and Monday edition, quoting a source close to talks.

"Suez and Lyonnaise des Eaux seem resolved to carry out this merger, but not at any price. If certain Suez shareholders go too far, they would prefer to cancel rather than get involved in something removing value or implying dismemberment."
A Suez spokeswoman declined to comment on the Le Monde article and Lyonnaise des Eaux was unavailable for comment.
Both sides have pledged to say nothing further after ending more than a week of market speculation about merger talks last Friday, when they announced the special April 11 board meetings.

But French media commentators, who had expected merger plans to be handled by regular board sessions at both companies this week, interpreted the move as a postponement and said the plan had run into strong resistance from a group of Suez investors.
"The fact is that the talks with shareholders are difficult," Le Monde said.

Le Figaro daily said that the head of French glassmaker Saint-Gobain, Jean-Louis Beffa, with 6.2 percent of Suez and egged on by his own biggest shareholder Generale des Eaux, was particularly reluctant to back a merger.

Utilities empire Generale is Lyonnaise's strongest business rival and although it has said it will not block a merger, its chairman Jean-Marie Messier is reported to be applying pressure behind the scenes to delay or at least limit the impact of one.
Also seen at odds with the plan is Banque Nationale de Paris (BNP), which bought its Suez shares at a high price in 1994 and 1995 and wants a bigger premium for its investment.

This week's board meetings -- on April 1 at Suez and April 2 at Lyonnaise -- are meant to finalise the 1996 accounts, which in Suez's case look likely to show the group swinging back to full-year profits after provisions for property losses in 1995.
Analysts expect the company, which sold its investment bank Banque Indosuez last year, to show a 1996 net profit of 1.15 billion francs after a 1995 net loss of 3.96 billion francs.
Utilitities group Lyonnaise said last month it did not expect surprises in its 1996 results, following earlier predictions they would match first-half growth of 25 percent.
In 1995, Lyonnaise posted a net attributable profit of 906 million francs, down 15 percent from the previous year.
A merger would put the companies among the top 10 by French market capitalisation, worth almost 80 billion francs on the Paris bourse although still behind rival Generale des Eaux.
Shares in Suez and Lyonnaise have risen 30 percent and 21 percent respectively this year. They closed at 290.5 francs and 575 francs on Thursday, the last trading day before Easter.

Analysts say it makes sense to merge the two, Lyonnaise with its sprawling empire in water distribution, electricity and construction, and Suez, a conglomerate seeking a raison d'etre after selling off the prestigious Indosuez and other key assets.
